paras: The threatened lynching of Jimmy Gates took place at Boise City, Idaho Territory, on November 28, 1880, when a large crowd surrounded Gates, accused of stabbing a packer, and threatened to hang him. Officers got him to jail with difficulty, and Pacific Coast papers carried the story as a short telegraphic item. No paper gives the race of Gates or of the wounded man.

According to the Idaho Semi-Weekly World, the stabbing happened at 4 o'clock on Sunday morning in a Boise City saloon, later named as Early's, while the men were playing high-ball poker. Gates was said to have been standing behind the other man's shoulder when he reached around and stabbed him in the abdomen, a wound the paper put at six inches deep. The Boise dispatch called Gates 'a San Francisco hoodlum' and the assault 'unprovoked', and the Idaho paper likewise saw nothing to provoke it.

Gates fled after the stabbing but was caught about 4 o'clock that afternoon at a 'China house' near the Boise River bridge, half a mile south of town. There a large crowd gathered around him at once and threatened to hang him, and the dispatch said it was 'hard work for the officers' to take him to jail. Even after he was locked up, the correspondent reported 'apprehension that a mob will break the jail open and hang him', and the Idaho Semi-Weekly World wrote of 'strong talk of lynching'.

No attack on the jail is reported in the coverage. On December 3 the Idaho Semi-Weekly World reported that the wounded man was still alive and that hopes were entertained for his recovery. In March 1881 an Ada County item credited to the Boise Democrat said 'young Gates' was still confined for the stabbing and that he and fellow prisoner Henry McDonald had freed one leg each by cutting their shackles before being re-ironed under greater vigilance. No report of an indictment or trial was found.

The Boise City dispatch of November 28 ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under the head 'Fatally Stabbed' and in the Eureka Daily Sentinel two days later, and condensed versions appeared in the Pioche Weekly Record and other Western papers into mid-December. Brief summaries in Sacramento, Phoenix and Lewiston reduced the event to a fatal stabbing and did not mention the crowd. The Portland New Northwest kept the lynching threat, saying the police 'had hard work to prevent the lynching of the murderer', though the wounded man was not known to have died.

The Idaho Semi-Weekly World, the nearest paper in the coverage, gave the fuller local story in its news column and followed the wounded man's condition without comment on the crowd. No paper gave the race of either man or framed the episode in racial terms.

The wire copy named the stabbed packer George Kennedy, while the Idaho Semi-Weekly World, in three items through March 1881, called him Geo. Cannady. Wire reports said he would die or had been 'fatally stabbed', but the later local report of December 3 found him alive and possibly recovering.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jimmy Gates
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd surrounded Gates on his recapture and threatened to hang him, and officers had to escort him to jail through it (A2, A4, A12); there was 'strong talk of lynching' (A5).
A 'large crowd' threatened to hang Gates over the stabbing, but officers got him to jail and no report says he was harmed (A2, A4, A8); this was a threatened lynching, not a killing.

The syndicated Boise dispatch (A2, A4, A12) and the independent Idaho Semi-Weekly World account (A5) agree on the stabbing, Gates's arrest and lynching talk, though they differ on the stabbed man's name.

accounts.label: Boise City telegraphic dispatch
accounts.gist: Kennedy, a packer, was stabbed without provocation by Jimmy Gates, who fled, was caught about 4 p.m. at a China house near the Boise River bridge, and was threatened with hanging by a large crowd; officers had hard work to get him to jail, and a jail break by a mob was feared.

accounts.label: Idaho Semi-Weekly World (local)
accounts.gist: Cannady was stabbed in a Boise City saloon at 4 o'clock Sunday morning during high-ball poker; there was strong talk of lynching and Gates was arrested; by Dec. 3 Cannady was alive and expected to recover.

framing.detail: Pacific Coast papers ran the Boise dispatch under heads such as 'Fatally Stabbed', calling Gates a 'San Francisco hoodlum' and the assault 'unprovoked'.
The New Northwest's one-line brief called Gates 'the murderer' and credited the police with preventing the lynching.
The Idaho Semi-Weekly World reported the lynching talk in a local news column without comment and followed the stabbed man's condition.

conflicts.note: The Idaho paper, local and repeated over four months (including a Boise Democrat item), uses Cannady; the wire uses Kennedy. Likely the same man.
The later local report is the better evidence for his condition on Dec. 3; no later report of his death or recovery was found.
Compatible; the wire gives 4 o'clock in the afternoon as the time of recapture.
